entries.sourceText: - **201. Twenty questions** \[Measure\]: 20 yes/no questions can pin down one of about a million things, if each splits the options in half.
entries.title: Twenty balanced questions
entries.lens: the maximum number of distinct answer strings

entries.sourceText: - **202. Wordle opener** \[Predict\]: rank first guesses by how much information they reveal on average.
entries.title: One feedback split in a word game
entries.lens: the average information of a binary feedback partition

entries.sourceText: - **203. Guess Who** \[Predict\]: "Does your person wear glasses?" vs a question that splits the board 50/50.
entries.title: Ask the balanced board question
entries.lens: the expected information of a yes-no split

entries.sourceText: - **204. Bits of surprise** \[Slider\]: a 1-in-2 event carries 1 bit; a 1-in-1,000 event about 10 bits.
entries.title: Bits in a surprising outcome
entries.lens: the logarithm of a specified event probability

entries.sourceText: - **205. Password strength** \[Measure\]: type a password pattern and see its entropy and time-to-crack.
entries.title: A uniform password model
entries.lens: the independence assumption behind password entropy

entries.sourceText: - **206. Compress this** \[Predict\]: which compresses more, a random string or a song chorus?
entries.title: Repetition lowers source entropy
entries.lens: the entropy rate of a stated binary source

entries.sourceText: - **207. Build a Huffman code** \[Slider\]: give common letters short codes and watch the message shrink.
entries.title: Give the frequent symbol fewer bits
entries.lens: frequency-weighted prefix-code length

entries.sourceText: - **208. Morse is efficient** \[Gotcha\]: E, the most common English letter, gets the shortest code, a single dot.
entries.title: A short code for the common symbol
entries.lens: the probability weight of a short code

entries.sourceText: - **209. Guess the next letter** \[Measure\]: play Shannon's game; English carries only about 1 bit per letter.
entries.title: A predictable next character
entries.lens: surprisal in a stated next-character model

entries.sourceText: - **210. KL divergence** \[Slider\]: drag one distribution away from another and watch the "surprise cost" grow, unevenly in each direction.
entries.title: Reverse the KL arguments
entries.lens: the weighting distribution in directional divergence

entries.sourceText: - **211. Cross-entropy loss** \[Slider\]: see why a confident wrong prediction is punished so much harder than a hesitant one.
entries.title: Confident and wrong costs more
entries.lens: the probability assigned to the observed class

entries.sourceText: - **212. Zero correlation, full dependence** \[Gotcha\]: y = x² has zero correlation with x, yet mutual information shows they're tied.
entries.title: Zero correlation can hide a function
entries.lens: linear correlation versus deterministic dependence

entries.sourceText: - **213. Noisy channel** \[Slider\]: add noise to a message and add repetition until it gets through.
entries.title: Three noisy copies and a majority
entries.lens: independent correctness in a toy repetition channel

entries.sourceText: - **214. Damaged QR code** \[Predict\]: cover more and more of a QR code; error correction keeps it readable up to about 30%.
entries.title: Code distance sets an error bound
entries.lens: symbol errors rather than covered image area

entries.sourceText: - **215. Twelve coins** \[Predict\]: find the fake coin in 3 weighings; each weighing gives 3 outcomes, and 3³ = 27 ≥ 24 cases.
entries.title: Three outcomes per weighing
entries.lens: the information capacity of a balance-scale answer

entries.sourceText: - **216. 1,000 poisoned bottles** \[Gotcha\]: 10 tasters can find the one poisoned bottle using binary codes.
entries.title: Binary labels for poisoned bottles
entries.lens: the number of binary taster-result patterns

entries.sourceText: - **217. How diverse is your week?** \[Measure\]: compute the entropy of your music, meals or commute routes.
entries.title: A two-option week has an entropy
entries.lens: diversity under a stated two-category frequency model

entries.sourceText: - **218. Maximum entropy die** \[Slider\]: if a die averages 4.5, what's the least-assuming distribution of its faces?
entries.title: A die constrained by its mean
entries.lens: the mean constraint in an exponential maximum-entropy family

entries.sourceText: - **219. Is the test worth it?** \[Slider\]: see how much a test reduces your uncertainty about a diagnosis.
entries.title: A test reduces average uncertainty
entries.lens: information averaged over positive and negative results

entries.sourceText: - **220. Hash collisions** \[Gotcha\]: with N possible hashes, collisions start around √N items, the birthday paradox again.
entries.title: A small hash space still collides
entries.lens: the birthday event in a finite uniform hash space

entries.sourceText: - **221. Green jelly beans** \[Gotcha\]: test 20 colors against acne; one comes out "significant" by chance.
entries.title: Twenty chances for a false discovery
entries.lens: family-wise error under independent null tests

entries.sourceText: - **222. p-hacking playground** \[Slider\]: drop outliers, add covariates, split subgroups until noise hits p < 0.05.
entries.title: Many analysis paths add opportunities
entries.lens: a union-bound ceiling rather than a fitted p-hacking simulator

entries.sourceText: - **223. Peeking** \[Predict\]: check an A/A test after every 100 users and stop at the first p < 0.05; false positives soar past 5%.
entries.title: Repeated opportunities need a model
entries.lens: a conservative bound without assuming independent repeated looks

entries.sourceText: - **224. What does p mean?** \[Split\]: poll common definitions; most popular answers are wrong.
entries.title: A p-value under a specified null
entries.lens: the null-tail event rather than probability of the null

entries.sourceText: - **225. Dance of the p-values** \[Predict\]: rerun the same real experiment 20 times; p jumps from 0.001 to 0.4.
entries.title: The count changes across repetitions
entries.lens: the tail probability as realized data vary

entries.sourceText: - **226. Statistical power** \[Slider\]: shrink the sample and watch a real effect go undetected most of the time.
entries.title: Power for a stated rejection rule
entries.lens: the detection probability under a specified alternative

entries.sourceText: - **227. Winner's curse** \[Gotcha\]: in small studies, the results that reach significance overstate the true effect.
entries.title: Select only the large estimates
entries.lens: outcome-dependent inclusion in a toy study collection

entries.sourceText: - **228. Many tests at once** \[Slider\]: compare no correction, Bonferroni and false-discovery-rate control on 100 tests.
entries.title: Bonferroni changes the threshold
entries.lens: the independent-test family rejection probability

entries.sourceText: - **229. Lady tasting tea** \[Measure\]: identify milk-first cups among 8; Fisher's original permutation test scores you.
entries.title: Milk-first cups under random guessing
entries.lens: the fixed-margin tail of a random allocation

entries.sourceText: - **230. Forking paths** \[Gotcha\]: one dataset, many reasonable analysis choices, wildly different conclusions.
entries.title: Forks create more possible analyses
entries.lens: the number of false-alarm opportunities

entries.sourceText: - **231. The dead salmon** \[Story\]: an fMRI scan of a dead fish showed "brain activity" without multiple-comparison correction (Bennett et al., 2009).
entries.title: Null voxels can still light up
entries.lens: multiple testing under an all-null toy scan

entries.sourceText: - **232. Significant but tiny** \[Slider\]: grow the sample to millions and a trivial effect becomes highly significant.
entries.title: A tiny effect with a huge sample
entries.lens: the standard error behind statistical separation

entries.sourceText: - **233. Shuffle test** \[Slider\]: shuffle group labels thousands of times to see how unusual the real difference is.
entries.title: Shuffle labels while keeping margins
entries.lens: the randomization distribution with fixed totals

entries.sourceText: - **234. Is your die fair?** \[Measure\]: roll 60 times and run a chi-square test on the counts.
entries.title: Three pairs of die faces
entries.lens: the Pearson statistic for three grouped categories

entries.sourceText: - **235. One tail or two?** \[Split\]: the same data is significant under one choice and not the other.
entries.title: One tail versus two tails
entries.lens: the disjoint tail events included in a test

entries.sourceText: - **236. HARKing** \[Gotcha\]: forming the hypothesis after seeing results makes any pattern look predicted.
entries.title: Choose a hypothesis after the search
entries.lens: the hidden search opportunity behind a selected pattern

entries.sourceText: - **237. Why 0.05?** \[Story\]: the threshold traces largely to a convenient choice in Fisher's 1925 textbook.
entries.title: Five percent is an input
entries.lens: the chosen nominal threshold under a null model

entries.sourceText: - **238. Show the interval** \[Slider\]: two studies with the same p-value can have very different effect sizes and certainty.
entries.title: The same z score at different scales
entries.lens: the effect scale and interval width

entries.sourceText: - **239. How many findings are true?** \[Slider\]: set prior odds and power; at low values most significant findings are false (Ioannidis, 2005).
entries.title: How many selected findings are true?
entries.lens: the prior share of true alternatives and test power

entries.sourceText: - **240. A/A test** \[Predict\]: compare two identical versions 100 times; about 5 come out "significant".
entries.title: False rejections in one hundred tests
entries.lens: the expected count under a specified null rejection rate

entries.sourceText: - **242. Overfitting** \[Slider\]: raise polynomial degree; training error drops while new-data error explodes.
entries.title: Training fit is not prediction error
entries.lens: bias and variance in an explicit error decomposition

entries.sourceText: - **243. Bias vs variance** \[Split\]: four dartboards: accurate, precise, both, neither.
entries.title: Accuracy and precision contribute
entries.lens: squared bias versus sampling variance

entries.sourceText: - **245. Cross-validation** \[Predict\]: pick the best model on held-out folds, then compare to the one that fit training data best.
entries.title: Compare estimated new-data errors
entries.lens: the risk decomposition rather than training fit alone

entries.sourceText: - **246. Ridge regression** \[Slider\]: increase the penalty and watch wild coefficients shrink toward zero.
entries.title: A penalty shrinks one coefficient
entries.lens: the ridge denominator in a centered single-feature model

entries.sourceText: - **247. One bad point** \[Slider\]: drag a single outlier and watch the least-squares line swing while a robust line holds.
entries.title: One point pulls the mean
entries.lens: the influence of an extreme observation

entries.sourceText: - **248. A billionaire walks in** \[Gotcha\]: the bar's average wealth skyrockets; the median barely moves.
entries.title: The billionaire changes the average
entries.lens: the mean and median of a fixed toy sample

entries.sourceText: - **249. Fish in a lake** \[Predict\]: tag 50 fish, recapture 50, count tagged ones, estimate the total.
entries.title: Tagged fish in the second sample
entries.lens: the recaptured tagged fraction under a closed-population model

entries.sourceText: - **252. Women outrunning men by 2156** \[Story\]: extending sprint-record trends gave that forecast (Tatem et al., 2004), a lesson in extrapolation.
entries.title: A straight trend beyond the data
entries.lens: the unsupported persistence of an extrapolated slope

entries.sourceText: - **253. Fermi estimates** \[Measure\]: estimate piano tuners in Berlin with ranges at each step and see the final uncertainty.
entries.title: Multiply ranges in a Fermi estimate
entries.lens: positive-factor bounds rather than a confidence interval

entries.sourceText: - **254. The ox at the fair** \[Story\]: the median of about 800 guesses was within 1% of the ox's weight (Galton, 1907).
entries.title: A crowd estimate against a benchmark
entries.lens: the signed error of a stated aggregate guess

entries.sourceText: - **255. You vs the crowd** \[Measure\]: guess jellybeans in a jar; see how the crowd average beats most individuals.
entries.title: A stated blend of crowd estimates
entries.lens: the weights behind a pooled numerical guess

entries.sourceText: - **256. Stein's paradox** \[Story\]: shrinking each baseball player's early average toward the group mean predicted the season better (Efron & Morris, 1975).
entries.title: Pull early averages toward the group
entries.lens: the evidence weight in a toy shrinkage estimator

entries.sourceText: - **258. Bandwidth** \[Slider\]: the same data looks unimodal or bimodal depending on kernel bandwidth.
entries.title: A bandwidth changes local information
entries.lens: the local sample-size facet of a smoothing tradeoff

entries.sourceText: - **259. Histogram bins lie** \[Slider\]: change bin width and a pattern appears or disappears.
entries.title: Histogram counts need their widths
entries.lens: the count per unit bin width in a density display

entries.sourceText: - **260. Stacking errors** \[Slider\]: combine uncertain measurements and watch how errors add in quadrature.
entries.title: Independent measurement errors combine
entries.lens: the addition of independent variances

entries.sourceText: - **261. Ice cream and drownings** \[Gotcha\]: both rise together; summer heat drives both.
entries.title: A common summer cause
entries.lens: the common-cause path in a stipulated structural model

entries.sourceText: - **262. Nicolas Cage and pool drownings** \[Gotcha\]: two unrelated yearly series track each other closely by pure coincidence (Vigen).
entries.title: Search enough unrelated series
entries.lens: the search opportunity behind a selected coincidence

entries.sourceText: - **263. Chocolate and Nobel prizes** \[Story\]: countries eating more chocolate have more Nobel laureates per capita (Messerli, 2012).
entries.title: A wealth proxy can predict both
entries.lens: the observational slope with a shared background cause

entries.sourceText: - **264. Storks and babies** \[Story\]: European stork populations correlate with birth rates (Matthews, 2000).
entries.title: Population size can drive both counts
entries.lens: the common scale factor behind two observed variables

entries.sourceText: - **265. More firefighters, more damage** \[Gotcha\]: bigger fires bring more firefighters and more damage.
entries.title: Severe fires bring both responses
entries.lens: the common severity cause and the intervention derivative

entries.sourceText: - **266. Shoe size and reading** \[Gotcha\]: in children, bigger feet predict better reading because both grow with age.
entries.title: Age connects two childhood measures
entries.lens: the shared age path in a structural toy model

entries.sourceText: - **267. Hospitals are deadly?** \[Gotcha\]: people in hospitals die more because sick people go to hospitals.
entries.title: Sicker people select into hospital
entries.lens: selection by a common severity variable

entries.sourceText: - **268. Correlation fishing** \[Slider\]: scan 1,000 random variables and find a few with r above 0.9.
entries.title: Fishing across a thousand variables
entries.lens: the multiplicity of a stipulated correlation search

entries.sourceText: - **271. Coffee and heart disease** \[Slider\]: toggle smoking as a hidden variable and watch coffee's "effect" disappear.
entries.title: A smoking confounder in a toy model
entries.lens: the open common-cause path before an intervention

entries.sourceText: - **272. Breakfast and weight** \[Split\]: half see the observational link, half see trial results; compare conclusions.
entries.title: An observed breakfast association
entries.lens: the difference between observing and assigning a behavior

entries.sourceText: - **273. Pirates and global warming** \[Gotcha\]: pirate numbers fell as temperatures rose, a classic parody chart.
entries.title: Two trends can co-move without cause
entries.lens: a stipulated time trend rather than a causal link

entries.sourceText: - **274. Shoes on in bed** \[Gotcha\]: sleeping in shoes predicts headaches; the hidden cause is a night of drinking.
entries.title: A night out is a common cause
entries.lens: the common background event in an observational association

entries.sourceText: - **275. Guess the correlation** \[Measure\]: see scatterplots and guess r; get your accuracy score.
entries.title: Translate a correlation carefully
entries.lens: the explained share in a simple linear regression

entries.sourceText: - **277. Anscombe's quartet** \[Gotcha\]: four datasets with identical stats and totally different pictures.
entries.title: A summary can miss one strange point
entries.lens: the sensitivity hidden by a single numerical summary

entries.sourceText: - **278. Datasaurus** \[Gotcha\]: a dinosaur-shaped scatter shares its summary statistics with a dozen other shapes.
entries.title: Different point clouds can share means
entries.lens: the insufficiency of a mean to determine a data shape

entries.sourceText: - **280. Rich states, rich voters** \[Gotcha\]: in the US, richer states lean Democratic while richer individuals lean Republican (Gelman, 2008).
entries.title: Groups and people use different weights
entries.lens: aggregation across groups rather than individual causal inference

entries.sourceText: - **281. Kidney stones** \[Story\]: open surgery did better for both small and large stones, yet the other treatment looked better overall (Charig et al., 1986).
entries.title: Stone size changes the treatment mix
entries.lens: unequal difficulty weights despite a stratum-level advantage

entries.sourceText: - **282. Berkeley admissions** \[Story\]: women had lower admission rates overall in 1973, but most departments admitted women at equal or higher rates.
entries.title: Departments have different base rates
entries.lens: department composition behind an aggregate admission contrast

entries.sourceText: - **283. Jeter vs Justice** \[Story\]: Justice had the higher batting average in both 1995 and 1996; Jeter was higher over the two years combined.
entries.title: Season weights flip a batting average
entries.lens: at-bat weights across seasons

entries.sourceText: - **284. COVID fatality by country** \[Story\]: Italy's case fatality was higher than China's overall but lower in every age group (von Kügelgen et al., 2021).
entries.title: Age weights change a fatality average
entries.lens: the population age composition of a descriptive risk

entries.sourceText: - **285. Build a Simpson** \[Slider\]: drag group sizes and rates until the overall comparison flips.
entries.title: Build a composition reversal
entries.lens: group weights with unchanged within-group rates

entries.sourceText: - **286. Slopes that flip** \[Slider\]: within each group the trend is up; pooled, it points down.
entries.title: A pooled contrast can reverse
entries.lens: the mixture component of a pooled comparison

entries.sourceText: - **287. Exercise and cholesterol** \[Slider\]: across ages, exercise seems to raise cholesterol; within each age group it lowers it.
entries.title: Age mix can reverse a health contrast
entries.lens: the age-stratum weights before interpreting an aggregate

entries.sourceText: - **288. Which surgeon?** \[Split\]: one surgeon looks worse overall but is better for both low- and high-risk patients.
entries.title: A surgeon's risk mix matters
entries.lens: case difficulty in a toy surgeon comparison

entries.sourceText: - **290. Wages by education** \[Story\]: in the 2000s, the overall US median wage rose while it fell within every education group, as the workforce became more educated.
entries.title: A more educated workforce changes a mean
entries.lens: composition changes despite declining component means

entries.sourceText: - **291. Smokers survived longer?** \[Story\]: in the Whickham study, smokers had better 20-year survival overall, because they were younger (Appleton et al., 1996).
entries.title: Younger smokers in an aggregate sample
entries.lens: age composition versus a stratum-level disadvantage

entries.sourceText: - **292. Lord's paradox** \[Gotcha\]: two reasonable analyses of the same diet data give opposite answers.
entries.title: Baseline adjustment changes the contrast
entries.lens: the chosen pre-post comparison and identifying assumptions

entries.sourceText: - **294. Ad performance by device** \[Slider\]: a campaign wins on mobile and desktop but loses overall.
entries.title: Device mix changes an ad aggregate
entries.lens: mobile and desktop weights in a conversion comparison

entries.sourceText: - **295. Airline delays** \[Story\]: one airline had better on-time rates at every airport but worse overall, because of its hub's weather.
entries.title: Airports have different delay risks
entries.lens: the airport composition behind on-time rates

entries.sourceText: - **296. Birth-weight paradox** \[Story\]: among low-weight babies, those of smoking mothers had lower mortality, a selection artifact.
entries.title: Select on a shared birth-weight cause
entries.lens: selection on a common consequence in a binary toy graph

entries.sourceText: - **298. Average speed** \[Gotcha\]: 30 km/h out, 60 km/h back is an average of 40, not 45.
entries.title: Equal distances at unequal speeds
entries.lens: time weighting of an out-and-back speed

entries.sourceText: - **300. Vaccinated in hospital** \[Story\]: in Israel in 2021 many hospitalized patients were vaccinated, yet within each age group vaccines strongly protected.
entries.title: Hospital counts need age composition
entries.lens: the strata weights behind a hospital-risk aggregate

entries.sourceText: - **301. Wald's bombers** \[Story\]: armor the spots *without* bullet holes on returning planes, because hits there brought planes down.
entries.title: Only returning aircraft are counted
entries.lens: outcome-dependent survival into the observed sample

entries.sourceText: - **302. Berkson's paradox** \[Gotcha\]: among hospital patients, two unrelated diseases look negatively correlated.
entries.title: Two diseases in a selected hospital
entries.lens: conditioning on a shared admission consequence

entries.sourceText: - **303. Attractive and mean?** \[Gotcha\]: if you only date people who are attractive or kind, looks and kindness seem opposed in your pool.
entries.title: Select people who pass either screen
entries.lens: the selection rule creating an apparent tradeoff

entries.sourceText: - **304. Collider slider** \[Slider\]: select only cases where X + Y is high and a fake negative correlation appears.
entries.title: Condition on X or Y being high
entries.lens: the binary OR version of collider selection

entries.sourceText: - **305. Talent vs fame** \[Slider\]: among famous actors, looks and acting skill appear unrelated or inversely related.
entries.title: A fame threshold selects either cause
entries.lens: selection on a common consequence of two traits

entries.sourceText: - **306. Dead funds vanish** \[Gotcha\]: average fund returns look better because closed, failed funds drop out of the data.
entries.title: Failed funds leave the database
entries.lens: outcome-dependent inclusion in a fund-return average

entries.sourceText: - **307. They built them better** \[Gotcha\]: old buildings seem sturdier because the flimsy ones already fell down.
entries.title: The weak buildings have disappeared
entries.lens: retention differences in a surviving-building sample

entries.sourceText: - **308. High-rise cats** \[Story\]: cats falling from higher floors seemed to survive better, partly because dead cats weren't taken to vets (Whitney & Mehlhaff, 1987).
entries.title: A veterinary sample omits some outcomes
entries.lens: outcome-dependent inclusion in observed cases

entries.sourceText: - **309. Dropout billionaires** \[Gotcha\]: famous dropouts are memorable; the millions of dropouts who didn't get rich aren't.
entries.title: Famous dropouts are a selected subset
entries.lens: the missing denominator of unsuccessful cases

entries.sourceText: - **310. The 1936 Literary Digest poll** \[Story\]: 2.4 million responses predicted Landon; Roosevelt won a landslide. Sample size can't fix bias.
entries.title: A huge poll still has the wrong mix
entries.lens: selection composition rather than sampling noise alone

entries.sourceText: - **312. Healthy worker effect** \[Gotcha\]: workers in a hazardous job can look healthier than the public, since the sick can't work.
entries.title: Employment selects on underlying health
entries.lens: health-dependent inclusion in an employed sample

entries.sourceText: - **316. Do Oscar winners live longer?** \[Story\]: an early finding of extra years (Redelmeier & Singh, 2001) shrank after fixing immortal-time bias (Sylvestre et al., 2006).
entries.title: Crediting guaranteed survival time
entries.lens: the time denominator before causal interpretation

entries.sourceText: - **318. LinkedIn success stories** \[Gotcha\]: you see the founders who took the risk and won, not those who took it and lost.
entries.title: Success stories omit unsuccessful risks
entries.lens: outcome-dependent visibility in a founder sample

entries.sourceText: - **320. Height in the NBA** \[Gotcha\]: among pros, height barely predicts scoring, since short players only make it with exceptional skill.
entries.title: Either trait can pass a pro threshold
entries.lens: selection on a shared professional-entry consequence

entries.sourceText: - **321. Doctor's choice vs coin flip** \[Slider\]: let doctors pick who gets treated and the effect is biased; flip a coin and it's right.
entries.title: A clinician's choice is not assignment
entries.lens: the common severity path versus an intervention derivative

entries.sourceText: - **322. Randomization balances the unseen** \[Predict\]: randomize 1,000 people and check a hidden trait; the groups match.
entries.title: Random groups can differ by chance
entries.lens: expected balance rather than exact realized balance

entries.sourceText: - **323. How many users?** \[Slider\]: set baseline rate and effect size; see the sample size needed.
entries.title: Precision has a sample-size price
entries.lens: the half-width target of a stated normal approximation

entries.sourceText: - **326. Placebo** \[Split\]: half get a "focus booster" sound, half a neutral one; compare self-rated focus.
entries.title: Compare a toy placebo outcome
entries.lens: the spread behind a standardized mean contrast

entries.sourceText: - **327. Clever Hans** \[Story\]: a horse "did arithmetic" by reading its questioner's cues, until the questioner didn't know the answer.
entries.title: A cue can drive the apparent skill
entries.lens: the hidden cue in a structural toy model

entries.sourceText: - **338. Test yourself** \[Measure\]: run an n-of-1 trial on coffee and sleep with randomized days.
entries.title: Yesterday's treatment carries over
entries.lens: the prior-exposure imbalance in a current-day comparison

entries.sourceText: - **339. 41 shades of blue** \[Story\]: Google tested 41 blue tones for links to find the best-performing one.
entries.title: Forty-one candidates create a family
entries.lens: the independent-null multiplicity baseline

entries.sourceText: - **340. The $100 million headline** \[Story\]: a small ad-title change at Bing, ignored for months, raised revenue about 12% (Kohavi & Thomke, 2017).
entries.title: A small change on a revenue baseline
entries.lens: the base behind a relative revenue change

entries.sourceText: - **341. Seeing vs doing** \[Split\]: a falling barometer predicts storms; forcing the needle down doesn't cause one.
entries.title: Seeing a reading versus setting it
entries.lens: the observation-intervention distinction

entries.sourceText: - **342. Build a DAG** \[Slider\]: drag arrows between variables and the app highlights which ones to adjust for.
entries.title: Read a three-node causal path
entries.lens: conditioning on the middle node of a fork

entries.sourceText: - **344. Fork, chain, collider** \[Gotcha\]: three tiny graphs; controlling for the middle node fixes one, breaks one, and blocks the effect in the third.
entries.title: A collider behaves differently
entries.lens: conditioning on a collider rather than a noncollider

entries.sourceText: - **345. d-separation game** \[Measure\]: given a graph, say whether two variables are independent; score your streak.
entries.title: Which path stays active?
entries.lens: the d-connection test for one isolated chain

entries.sourceText: - **347. Table 2 fallacy** \[Gotcha\]: in one regression, each coefficient answers a different causal question, or none.
entries.title: A coefficient answers a partial question
entries.lens: the direct path versus the total intervention effect

entries.sourceText: - **352. Butterfly bias** \[Gotcha\]: one variable that is both a confounder and a collider; adjusting and not adjusting both bias.
entries.title: One adjustment choice is insufficient
entries.lens: the common-cause facet of a more complex adjustment problem

entries.sourceText: - **353. Controlling for the outcome's child** \[Gotcha\]: adjusting for a consequence of the outcome distorts the effect.
entries.title: Select on a consequence of the outcome
entries.lens: the selection facet of conditioning on downstream information

entries.sourceText: - **354. Bad control in pay gaps** \[Gotcha\]: controlling for occupation can hide discrimination that works through occupation.
entries.title: An occupation path is part of the total
entries.lens: the mediated component removed by holding a mediator fixed

entries.sourceText: - **356. The rooster and the sun** \[Gotcha\]: perfect prediction, zero causation.
entries.title: A rooster can predict without causing
entries.lens: a common clock variable rather than an intervention effect

entries.sourceText: - **360. Your decision graph** \[Measure\]: draw the causal graph behind a personal choice, like whether a gym habit improves sleep.
entries.title: State a model for the decision graph
entries.lens: the specified direct and mediated paths

entries.sourceText: - **361. Two worlds** \[Split\]: a split screen plays out the same person's life with and without a choice.
entries.title: Two outcomes for the same toy unit
entries.lens: the contrast between two modeled potential outcomes

entries.sourceText: - **363. Fill the table** \[Predict\]: guess the hidden outcomes, then reveal the true individual effects from a simulation.
entries.title: Fill the missing potential outcome
entries.lens: the individual effect in a fully specified toy table

entries.sourceText: - **365. Averages hide people** \[Slider\]: an average effect of zero can hide half helped and half harmed.
entries.title: Zero average can hide opposite effects
entries.lens: the subgroup mixture of treatment effects

entries.sourceText: - **366. Would she have lived?** \[Slider\]: estimate the probability the drug was necessary for survival, given trial and observational data.
entries.title: A structural survival counterfactual
entries.lens: the stipulated missing outcome rather than an identified individual claim

entries.sourceText: - **367. But-for causation** \[Split\]: poll a legal case; would the harm have happened anyway?
entries.title: Would the other cause suffice?
entries.lens: the OR structural rule behind a but-for contrast

entries.sourceText: - **368. Firing squad** \[Gotcha\]: two shooters fire; neither shot is "necessary", yet both caused the death.
entries.title: Two sufficient causes can overlap
entries.lens: the difference between necessity and sufficiency

entries.sourceText: - **369. Preemption** \[Gotcha\]: one assassin's poison would have worked, but the other's bullet got there first.
entries.title: The earlier event happens first
entries.lens: the timing rule that distinguishes a backup cause

entries.sourceText: - **370. Spillover breaks the table** \[Gotcha\]: your vaccination changes my outcome, so "my outcome if treated" isn't well defined.
entries.title: Your exposure includes treated neighbors
entries.lens: interference beyond a unit's own treatment

entries.sourceText: - **371. Counterfactual fairness** \[Slider\]: change only an applicant's group, hold everything causally downstream consistent, and see whether the decision changes.
entries.title: Keep the inferred disturbance fixed
entries.lens: the structural counterfactual rather than an arbitrary feature swap

entries.sourceText: - **372. What would flip the decision?** \[Slider\]: find the smallest change to an application that turns a loan denial into approval.
entries.title: A decision score crosses a threshold
entries.lens: the stipulated score rule rather than a causal fairness guarantee

entries.sourceText: - **373. Twin studies** \[Story\]: identical twins raised apart give a natural, if imperfect, look at counterfactual lives.
entries.title: Shared background and noisy measurement
entries.lens: the model-based weight of a noisy related observation

entries.sourceText: - **374. Model the missing outcome** \[Slider\]: train a model to predict outcomes with and without treatment and compare the two.
entries.title: Compare two predicted potential outcomes
entries.lens: the model-dependent imputation of an unobserved outcome

entries.sourceText: - **375. Monday-morning quarterback** \[Gotcha\]: judging a decision by its outcome confuses bad luck with bad choices.
entries.title: A good choice can still lose once
entries.lens: expected payoff rather than a single realized outcome

entries.sourceText: - **376. Weather butterfly** \[Slider\]: nudge starting conditions slightly and watch ensemble forecasts diverge.
entries.title: A small initial difference grows
entries.lens: the amplification assumed in a divergent toy recurrence

entries.sourceText: - **377. How much is due to smoking?** \[Slider\]: compute the share of lung cancer cases that wouldn't occur without smoking.
entries.title: An attributable fraction needs a model
entries.lens: exposure prevalence under a homogeneous causal risk-ratio model

entries.sourceText: - **378. Excess deaths** \[Story\]: pandemic death tolls were estimated by comparing actual deaths to a modeled no-pandemic baseline.
entries.title: Deaths versus a modeled baseline
entries.lens: the specified counterfactual baseline in an excess count

entries.sourceText: - **379. Heatwave attribution** \[Story\]: climate scientists compare simulated worlds with and without warming to say how much likelier a heatwave became.
entries.title: Compare two modeled event probabilities
entries.lens: the probability ratio across stipulated worlds

entries.sourceText: - **380. Three steps to a counterfactual** \[Slider\]: infer the hidden noise, change the cause, replay the model (Pearl's abduction–action–prediction).
entries.title: Infer noise, change X, replay Y
entries.lens: abduction and intervention in a stated linear equation

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **382. Broken parallel trends** \[Slider\]: tilt the control group's pre-trend and watch the estimate go wrong.
entries.title: The control trend changes the estimate
entries.lens: the untreated-trend assumption behind a difference-in-differences

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **383. Minimum wage in New Jersey** \[Story\]: fast-food employment didn't fall after NJ raised its minimum wage, compared with Pennsylvania (Card & Krueger, 1994).
entries.title: A toy neighboring-state comparison
entries.lens: the control change in a two-period policy comparison

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **384. Event study plot** \[Slider\]: plot effects by period before and after treatment; flat leads build trust, sloped ones raise flags.
entries.title: A pre-period check is another contrast
entries.lens: the pre-period trend diagnostic before causal interpretation

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **385. Staggered rollout trap** \[Gotcha\]: when units adopt at different times and effects grow, standard two-way fixed effects can even flip sign (Goodman-Bacon, 2021).
entries.title: Negative comparison weights can distort
entries.lens: the weighted-effect arithmetic behind problematic comparisons

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **387. Turning 21** \[Story\]: US mortality jumps right at the legal drinking age (Carpenter & Dobkin, 2009).
entries.title: Just below and above an age cutoff
entries.lens: the local outcome discontinuity under a threshold model

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **388. RDD bandwidth** \[Slider\]: widen the window around the cutoff and trade bias for noise.
entries.title: A wider cutoff window trades errors
entries.lens: the assumed bias-variance tradeoff in a local fit

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **389. Bunching at the line** \[Gotcha\]: a pile-up of cases just past a threshold reveals manipulation and breaks the design.
entries.title: Counts bunch on one side of a cutoff
entries.lens: a descriptive density imbalance near an assignment line

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **390. The draft lottery** \[Story\]: random draft numbers let researchers measure military service's effect on earnings (Angrist, 1990).
entries.title: An assignment changes service uptake
entries.lens: the first-stage denominator in a toy IV estimate

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **392. Weak instrument** \[Slider\]: shrink the instrument's pull on treatment and the estimate goes wild.
entries.title: A weak first stage amplifies the ratio
entries.lens: the sensitivity of the Wald ratio to weak uptake

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **393. Exclusion violated** \[Gotcha\]: if the instrument affects the outcome through another path, IV quietly fails.
entries.title: An extra outcome path contaminates IV
entries.lens: the reduced-form numerator under a violated exclusion story

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **394. California tobacco tax** \[Story\]: a synthetic California built from other states showed Proposition 99 cut cigarette sales (Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller, 2010).
entries.title: Actual minus a synthetic donor mix
entries.lens: the donor weights defining a model-based counterfactual

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **396. Interrupted time series** \[Slider\]: fit the trend before a policy and compare it with what came after.
entries.title: Project the pre-policy trend
entries.lens: the assumed continuation of a fitted pre-period slope

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **397. The Oregon lottery** \[Story\]: Medicaid access was assigned by lottery in 2008, letting researchers measure its effects (Finkelstein et al., 2012).
entries.title: A lottery offer is not full take-up
entries.lens: the intention-to-treat change divided by the uptake change

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **398. Kink design** \[Slider\]: a change in slope at a threshold, like a benefit formula's kink, identifies an effect.
entries.title: A slope change divided by a first stage
entries.lens: the ratio of stipulated local slope changes

entries.sourceSection: 20. Natural experiments: IV, RDD, diff-in-diff, synthetic control
entries.sourceText: - **399. Distance to college** \[Story\]: growing up near a college served as an instrument for schooling's effect on earnings (Card, 1995).
entries.title: A stipulated college-distance instrument
entries.lens: the first stage and untested exclusion assumptions

entries.sourceText: - **402. Overlap histograms** \[Slider\]: plot propensity scores for both groups; slide confounding up until the humps separate.
entries.title: Count supported toy strata
entries.lens: the observed treatment support within strata

entries.sourceText: - **403. No overlap, no answer** \[Gotcha\]: if every rich person was treated and no poor one was, the data can't tell you the effect.
entries.title: An empty assignment cell
entries.lens: the distinction between support and extrapolation

entries.sourceText: - **404. Weighted bubbles** \[Slider\]: inverse-probability weights resize each dot until both groups look alike.
entries.title: A weighted unit changes its influence
entries.lens: the inverse assignment probability of an observed unit

entries.sourceText: - **405. Exploding weights** \[Gotcha\]: one person with a 1% treatment chance who got treated counts as 100 people.
entries.title: One rare assignment gets a large weight
entries.lens: the scale of a positivity-near-boundary weight

entries.sourceText: - **406. LaLonde's benchmark** \[Story\]: many observational methods failed to recover a job-training program's experimental effect (LaLonde, 1986).
entries.title: A method versus a trial benchmark
entries.lens: the numerical estimation error against a stipulated benchmark

entries.sourceText: - **407. How strong a hidden confounder?** \[Slider\]: the E-value shows how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to erase a result.
entries.title: A risk-ratio sensitivity function
entries.lens: the stated confounding sensitivity function

entries.sourceText: - **409. Love plot** \[Slider\]: watch covariate imbalances shrink toward zero as matching improves.
entries.title: Balance on a common covariate scale
entries.lens: the observed standardized mean difference

entries.sourceText: - **410. Coarsened matching** \[Slider\]: group ages into bands and match exactly within them.
entries.title: Coarsen ages into explicit bands
entries.lens: the grouping boundary used for a coarsened match

entries.sourceText: - **411. Regression vs matching** \[Split\]: two methods, same data; see where they agree and where extrapolation bites.
entries.title: A regression beyond the matched region
entries.lens: the prediction outside an observed comparison region

entries.sourceText: - **412. Peeking at outcomes** \[Gotcha\]: tuning the matching while looking at results quietly turns it into p-hacking.
entries.title: Outcome-guided tuning creates a search
entries.lens: the multiplicity facet of selecting an analysis by outcomes

entries.sourceText: - **413. Propensity score paradox** \[Gotcha\]: matching on propensity scores can increase imbalance after a point (King & Nielsen, 2019).
entries.title: A matching procedure can worsen balance
entries.lens: the realized covariate balance rather than a method label

entries.sourceText: - **414. Entropy balancing** \[Slider\]: solve for weights that match group means exactly.
entries.title: Choose weights to hit one target mean
entries.lens: the support and moment constraint of a two-point balance

entries.sourceText: - **415. Caliper width** \[Slider\]: tighter matches mean fewer matched pairs; see the trade-off live.
entries.title: A tighter caliper drops a pair
entries.lens: the distance threshold for retaining a toy match

entries.sourceText: - **416. Trimming changes the question** \[Gotcha\]: dropping hard-to-match people changes *whose* effect you estimate.
entries.title: Trimming changes whose average is taken
entries.lens: the population mixture after excluding a subgroup

entries.sourceText: - **417. Healthy-user bias** \[Gotcha\]: people who take preventive drugs also exercise and eat well, inflating apparent benefits.
entries.title: Healthy behavior predicts both choices
entries.lens: the common background cause behind an observed benefit

entries.sourceText: - **418. Flu shots before flu season** \[Story\]: vaccinated seniors also died less *before* flu season, a sign of confounding (Jackson et al., 2006).
entries.title: An association before the season
entries.lens: the common-cause explanation of a negative-control association

entries.sourceText: - **419. Rosenbaum bounds** \[Slider\]: dial up hidden bias until a matched study's conclusion breaks.
entries.title: Hidden odds in a matched pair
entries.lens: the assignment-probability bound under a stated Gamma

entries.sourceText: - **420. Target trial emulation** \[Story\]: design an observational analysis as if it were a trial you could have run (Hernán & Robins, 2016).
entries.title: State the comparison before fitting
entries.lens: the explicit time and comparison structure of a toy target trial

entries.sourceText: - **421. Four kinds of customers** \[Split\]: persuadables, sure things, lost causes and sleeping dogs; guess which a coupon should target.
entries.title: Some customers move, others do not
entries.lens: the mixture of causal response types

entries.sourceText: - **422. Uplift vs propensity** \[Slider\]: target the likeliest buyers vs those most *changed* by the offer, and compare revenue.
entries.title: High propensity is not high uplift
entries.lens: incremental net value rather than baseline conversion

entries.sourceText: - **423. Qini curve** \[Slider\]: rank customers by predicted uplift and watch cumulative gains rise, then fall.
entries.title: Cumulative gains can turn negative
entries.lens: the incremental value of a marginal targeted group

entries.sourceText: - **424. Causal forest heatmap** \[Slider\]: the treatment effect painted across age and income.
entries.title: A stipulated effect surface along age
entries.lens: the age slice of a specified heterogeneous-effect model

entries.sourceText: - **425. Aspirin and star signs** \[Story\]: in the ISIS-2 trial, aspirin seemed not to help Geminis and Libras, a deliberate warning about subgroup fishing.
entries.title: Twelve null subgroups can mislead
entries.lens: the subgroup-search multiplicity under a toy null

entries.sourceText: - **426. Who should get it?** \[Slider\]: set a budget and a learned rule picks who benefits most from treatment.
entries.title: Spend a fixed treatment budget well
entries.lens: the stipulated causal lift net of treatment cost

entries.sourceText: - **427. Effect by age** \[Slider\]: the treatment effect as a curve over age, with a confidence band.
entries.title: A toy effect changes linearly with age
entries.lens: the slope assumption in an age-effect curve

entries.sourceText: - **428. Additive or multiplicative?** \[Gotcha\]: an interaction can exist on the risk-difference scale and vanish on the ratio scale.
entries.title: One ratio, unequal absolute differences
entries.lens: the effect scale used to describe interaction

entries.sourceText: - **429. Direct vs indirect** \[Slider\]: split a training program's effect into the part through new skills and the rest.
entries.title: Add the direct and mediator paths
entries.lens: the linear no-confounding mediation decomposition

entries.sourceText: - **430. Mediation's hidden trap** \[Gotcha\]: a confounder between mediator and outcome breaks the split, even in a randomized trial.
entries.title: A mediator association can be confounded
entries.lens: the common-cause facet missing from a naive mediation split

entries.sourceText: - **431. Coupon heterogeneity** \[Slider\]: a discount helps price-sensitive shoppers and wastes money on loyal ones.
entries.title: Coupon response differs across segments
entries.lens: the causal lift rather than loyalty alone

entries.sourceText: - **432. Paying sure things** \[Gotcha\]: discounts to customers who'd buy anyway look effective by naive metrics.
entries.title: Paying people who already would buy
entries.lens: the difference between baseline purchase and incremental lift

entries.sourceText: - **433. Sleeping dogs** \[Gotcha\]: a "we miss you" email reminds some subscribers to cancel.
entries.title: A message can have negative uplift
entries.lens: the signed incremental response to treatment

entries.sourceText: - **434. S, T and X learners** \[Split\]: three ways to estimate individual effects; compare their errors on simulated data.
entries.title: Compare toy effect-estimator errors
entries.lens: the bias-variance risk rather than an estimator's name

entries.sourceText: - **435. Number needed to treat** \[Slider\]: convert a risk reduction into how many people must be treated to help one.
entries.title: Convert an absolute risk reduction
entries.lens: the reciprocal risk difference under a stipulated causal model

entries.sourceText: - **436. "Doubles the risk"** \[Gotcha\]: from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 is a doubling, and still tiny.
entries.title: Doubling a tiny baseline risk
entries.lens: absolute versus relative risk change

entries.sourceText: - **437. Baseline risk matters** \[Slider\]: the same relative benefit helps high-risk patients far more in absolute terms.
entries.title: A common ratio meets different baselines
entries.lens: the baseline-dependent absolute effect

entries.sourceText: - **438. Scholarship policy** \[Slider\]: learn a rule for who gets aid to maximize graduations under a fixed budget.
entries.title: Allocate aid by graduation lift
entries.lens: the incremental benefit under a constrained policy budget

entries.sourceText: - **439. Average winner, segment loser** \[Gotcha\]: an A/B winner can hurt a key segment hidden in the average.
entries.title: An average can hide a harmed segment
entries.lens: the segment weights behind an average effect

entries.sourceText: - **440. Ad to search to sale** \[Slider\]: trace how much of an ad's effect works through branded searches.
entries.title: An ad can act through a search path
entries.lens: the direct and mediated terms in a toy path model

entries.sourceText: - **441. The rat-tail bounty** \[Story\]: colonial Hanoi paid per rat tail in 1902, and people began farming rats; a measure became a target.
entries.title: A bounty needs incremental outcomes
entries.lens: the causal objective rather than a paid activity count

entries.sourceText: - **442. Predictive policing loop** \[Slider\]: patrol where crime was recorded, record more crime there, repeat.
entries.title: Observed activity reinforces exposure
entries.lens: the amplification assumed in a feedback recurrence

entries.sourceText: - **443. Popularity loop** \[Slider\]: a recommender shows popular items, which get more clicks, which makes them more popular.
entries.title: Popularity feeds the next exposure
entries.lens: the recursive exposure rule in a toy popularity loop

entries.sourceText: - **444. Granger's rooster** \[Gotcha\]: crowing "Granger-causes" sunrise, since it reliably comes first.
entries.title: A shared clock predicts both signals
entries.lens: prediction through a common cause without intervention effect

entries.sourceText: - **445. Delayed effects** \[Slider\]: shift the lag and a cause that seemed useless shows a clear effect weeks later.
entries.title: A delayed effect enters the comparison
entries.lens: the alignment of lagged exposure and current outcome

entries.sourceText: - **446. Friedman's thermostat** \[Gotcha\]: heater use correlates with cold rooms, though the heater is what keeps them from being colder.
entries.title: A thermostat reacts to the cold
entries.lens: feedback selection versus a stipulated heating intervention

entries.sourceText: - **447. Herd immunity** \[Slider\]: vaccinate a share of a network and watch unvaccinated people get protected too.
entries.title: Neighbors receive an indirect benefit
entries.lens: the neighborhood exposure in an interference model

entries.sourceText: - **448. Leaky A/B test** \[Gotcha\]: treated users share a feature with control friends, shrinking the measured effect.
entries.title: Controls share some treated exposure
entries.lens: contamination of a unit-level treatment contrast

entries.sourceText: - **449. Stolen sales** \[Gotcha\]: boosting treated sellers in a marketplace test steals buyers from control sellers, doubling the apparent lift.
entries.title: A control loss enlarges measured lift
entries.lens: market displacement versus a treated-control gap

entries.sourceText: - **450. Switchback tests** \[Slider\]: alternate the whole market between versions by time slot instead of splitting users.
entries.title: A switchback still has carryover
entries.lens: the prior-slot exposure left in a current-period contrast
